Hongkong, Thursday, Feb. 25, 1926.
WAIFS AND STRAYS.

During the Lenten season, the Cathedral devotes the self-narcificing offerings it receives to the little-known, but very excellent Society for helping Waifs and Strays. Waifs and strays! There is a poignancy about these words which drive the meaning of them home as nothing else but the sight of young human defelicts can. It comes with increased force and meaning when the cold wind of recent days makes the warmth of fires so doubly welcome; and when attention is drawn to the splendid work of the Hongkong Benevolent Society which looks after waifs and strays of an older growth. There may be little or no poverty in Hongkong. What there is seems to be well hidden. On the foreign side it possibly does not exist; and it is only by a study of the necessarily private reports of the Benevolent Society that we can realise the want which affects numbers who become stranded here and have no power of themselves to help themselves. Of the Chinese side of the question there is probably little to indicate what the exact position of affairs is, and how it is to be regarded. These beggar people, for instance. The idea of beggar guilds affronts the good taste of normally charitable people. Making a business of poverty and doing well out of it is not in keeping with charitable thoughts. So, when we read that so many beggars have been deported to “another place”, the news is taken as one of those things of life out here which must be accepted as it is, and which is being dealt with in the only manner possible in all the circumstances of difference of though and outlook. But there is another class of walf and stray to which the mind, at this cold season of the year instinctively turns. More often than not, the existence of this class is thrust upon our notice by the sight of things which

we gain would order differently. were it in our power to do so. It is no compliment to our boasted civilisation—be it Chinese or foreign—to see, as can be seen any night in Hongkong, bundles of humanity seeking repose in doorways, alleyways, and on sidewalks, covered only by some piece of dirty matting—seeking this repose in spite of rain and cold. It is disturbing. The one bright spot about this social sore, is that others are disturbed about the existence of this problem. We know that there are those—Chinese let it be said—who, without ostentation, seek to alleviate hardship by such things as the distribution of blankets. We believe there is a tendency to regard this particular problem as insoluble—that, probably it is mixed up with the shifting nature of the work which this class of derelict does. It may be so. But we cannot get away from the fact that the problem does not seem to have been seriously tackled. We are not much concerned as to whose duty it is to give it attention; but we can point out that here is another matter on which Chinese and foreign can find a common interest of unity.

LABOUR COUNTESS
GIVES AWAY HER COUNTRY HOUSE.
TRADE UNION'S WINDFALL

The Counters of Warwick, who has long been associated with the Labour movement, to day handed over Easton Lodge, her country house in Essex with 900 acres of land, to the Labour Party for use as a trade union centre.
The Trade Union Congress, in thanking the Countess, declared that her magnificent gift would be devoted to the progress and development of the Trade Union movement on educational lines.

A tragic fate overtook a number of Chinese who had used as a private�ium den an unoccupied house at Cheung. Sha Wan on the route to Castle Peak.

Rendered still more dangerous by the recent rains, the building collapsed at 8:30 p.m. yesterday while the illicit opium smokers were congregated on the upper floor.

One man is reported to have extricated himself and bolted from the scene. Four others were partly buried in the ruins and were rescued by the Fire Brigade. They were taken to the Kwong Wah Hospital, but two of them succumbed to their injuries.
The work of searching the ruins for more victims was proceeding this morning.
CORRESPONDENCE
(To the Editor of the China Mail).
Sir,—I presume I am expected to accept the letter of your correspondent on this subject, as an apology. So be it; one soon learns not to expect much in this part of the world.

As regards the question of my experiences, which certainly seem to have aroused a lot more interest than I, as a modest and retiring kind of man, care to contemplate, it is difficult for me to enlarge on them in public in such a way as to bring all the story vividly before the eyes of the Public. It is seldom, in these prosaic times that anyone meets with an adventure that savours almost of the days of the Magic Carpet, and naturally I hesitate to lay myself open to a charge of out-doing Baron, Munchausen.
A few sympathetic friends have however stood by me when certain low fellows of the baser sort descended to jeering at my story which he it noted has been at

tracted from me piecemeal, and by no means with my willing consent. These friends assure me that it is actually my duty, and only in keeping with a promise I made previously—and I am very sorry I did make it now—to give the true version of my extraordinary experience in public. That being so I have completed all arrangements with a few of my comrades connected with me in this affair—who by a purely fortuitous chance happen to be in Hongkong at present—consisting of my wife and brother, the lady who might have been my wife, and others, together with the kind assistance of several more Hongkong people who are good enough to help me out owing to the great interest they take in the business.

"I have arranged to hold a series of public performances at the Theatre Royal starting on Tuesday next at 9:15 p.m. when I shall publicly explain with every aid that Art and Science can lend, all the experiences that follow from the moment I accepted the gift from All of a Jade Charm. The scenes vary between London and "Persia," to avoid appearing too egotistical. I have arranged some wonderful Dancing and music.

Now that I have screwed myself up to the pitch like this, I hope that the public will honour me with their company. If after they have heard all I have to say, they still think that I am a romancer—which is a much.milder term than any. I have heard used—I shall shake the dust of Hongkong off my feet with no regrets, and return to where I can find a little human appreciation.

Sir,—May I take the liberty of asking you to mention that as the entries for the Flower Show close at 1 o'clock next Monday, March 1, it is hoped that all those interested in horticulture will devote a part of this week-end in shroffing up their gardens with a view to sending in as many entries as possible. If there is any reasonable doubt as to whether any particular exhibit will be ready or good enough for the Show on March 11, Intending exhibitors should certainly enter same remembering that one week of fine weather can make all the difference to a garden.
Yours, etc.
E. B. C. HORNELL,
Hon. Secretary,
Hongkong Horticultural Society.
Hongkong Feb. 25

There must be quite a JAMES number who remember CANTLIE Dr. James Cantlie—friend of the late Dr. Sun Yat-sen—who spent many years in Hongkong—and of Dr. Manson. In an introduction to a recent book Dr. Cantlie tells how he came to practise in Hongkong.
SHREDS AND PATCHES.

One day in the Christmas holidays of 1886 he says, my friend Dr. John Mitchell Bruce, asked me if I could help him to find a doctor who could take the place of a great man who wished to return from the tropics. We knew of many young men, and discussed scores of those who might prove suitable. None, however, seemed quite to fit the situation, and we gave it up in despair.

Bruce, of course, knew the man who was writing home, but he would give me no clue of his identity nor tell me where he lived. I was then a teacher of anatomy at Charing Cross Hospital, where I had been lecturing seventeen years for a salary of £75 a year.
“Well, Bruce,” I said, “many a man I have taught and put on the road to success is now driving his carriage in London and earning a livelihood ten times as big as mine. I don’t see why I should not have a try for it myself. Where is it?”

"Well," I said, "we'll leave out Mars. If it is Australia, New Zealand, India, the Cape or America north or south, I am not going. But if it is Mackie's practice in Alexandria or Man-son's practice in Hongkong I am going."
“It is not Mackie's practice, but Manson's,” Bruce replied. “Good, I will go,” I answered. “But how are you going to live?” he said.
“That does not trouble me,” I replied, and half an hour later we wired to Manson: “Will Cantlie do?”
Twenty-four hours later THE ONE came back the reply: It WORD was the one word

only communication that passed between us, and in the month of June, 1887, I was in Hongkong. No financial arrangements were made and no stipulations set forth; and thus I found myself the partner of the great man I had never previously met nor spoken to in my life. Deliberately I avoided the topic of money, and it was three months before we discussed it, and I knew what I was to receive. Our association, started in this strange way, continued right up to Manson's death.
The outbreak of plague in Hongkong in the nineties found me in Vladivostok. The plague hospital was built of bamboo and palm, and had twenty-five beds.
“Since you have been here, eleven patients have died,” the doctor said.
In a short time all were dead. Another twenty-five plague patients were brought in
to take their places, and these, too soon passed away. Again the beds were filled, and it was not long before these twenty-five sufferers followed the other fifty to the grave.

We were absolutely ignorant of the plague, we knew nothing about it. One morning a clergy-man walked into my room, and we began to talk about the terrible scourge that was afficting Hongkong. I dwelt on our ignorance.
"You will find all you IN THE want to know about the BIBLE plague" in the Bible," he replied.
"Where?". I asked in amazement.
"In the First Book" of Samuel, chapters four, five and six," he answered.

I took the Bible and read how the Philistines sent back the Ark of the Covenant to the Israelites with two gifts to place the wrath of the God of Israel. These gifts were five golden emerods, or buboes, to signify the plague, and five golden rats—indisputable proof that the Philistines knew that the plague was caused by rats.
It is a most astonishing thing that the Bible should link the plague with rats, which in ancient days were regarded as large mice, and thus point the way to solve the mystery of the disease.
LITERATURE IN SCHOOLS.

The passage in the Bible which, in the light of modern knowledge, is so pregnant with meaning, reads: "What shall be the trespass offering which we shall return to him? They answered, five golden emerods, and five golden mice, according to the number of the lords of the Philistines: for one plague was on you all, and on your lords. Wherefore ye shall make images of your emerods, and images of your mice that mar the land; and ye shall give glory unto the God of Israel: peradventure he will lighten his hand from off you, and from off your gods, and from off your land."

In my youth times were not so easy as they are now. I know students going through the University who had barely enough money to buy salt for their kale. It was a desperate struggle for many of them. Some, unable to afford candles, were compelled to study at night by the light that entered the window from the street lamp outside.

Ever since the school began to take modern languages seriously there has been searching of heart among the pedagogues as to what French and German books should be read in class. It was not unnecessary. Some of us (says, the "Daily Telegraph") can remember being set down to volumes of elegant extracts from authors whose works we have never met since. There were, when Plancus was Consul, schools in which certain innocuous tales of the late M. Zola were chosen by an inscrutable Providence as the best introduction to French literature. Stalky and his young friends, it is recorded, had to wander through the sands of the "Roman d'un Jeune Homme Pauvre." Many generations since Major Pendennis was a child have been fed upon the edifying pages of "Télémaque." In the learning of German the works of Schiller, verse and prose, used to loom so large that he seemed to be the only German author. They have changed all that, or most of it, but even yet the headmasters cannot rest and be thankful Mr. H. Nicholson has been telling their assembled Conference that much of the stuff which is being read in modern languages is merely amusing and of no high literary value. He demands that every book chosen should be first rate; "not only should it be good literature, but it should deal with the history, art, and social conditions of the country whose language they were studying." When Yersin arrived in Hongkong I gave him a microscope and a deal of scientific bit, and my wife used to make the broth for his plague cultures. But it is not every language which has an Eschylus, a Dante, a Shakespeare. Perhaps Mr. Nicholson asks only that whatever is read should be first rate of its kind. This is in itself a sound and sufficiently practical principle. But we do not know how to reconcile it with the condition that the book must deal with "history, art, and social conditions." This would let in almost any good novel, but seems to exclude most of the best poetry. Whether Ronsard is writing a ballad or Racine a tragedy, their verses have nothing to say about social conditions or history, or any art but their own. There are, of course, schemes of education which would condemn such poetry. Dr. Arnold never could understand why people wanted to read poems the subjects of which seemed to him undignified. But though a schoolmaster must in the nature of things act on the assumption that he is always right, he had better not erect his private taste into a universal law. The most difficult problems in the choice of foreign books for class reading are not in excluding whatever is not valuable. The riches of those modern languages which are taught in schools are ample. But to choose such books as will rouse and stimulate children's interest in reading, while providing such mental exercise and discipline as their minds need and a store of knowledge and thoughts which will endure—this is none too easy in a world of unequal brains.
